title: The Woman in White’s Widow
author: William Saville
content:
Harrison Calloway sat in his creaking rocking chair, eyes dull, skin sagging like weathered parchment, as the sun dipped behind the hills. His old hands, knotted with arthritis, trembled as they rested on the arms of the chair, but it wasn’t being nearly one hundred years old that caused them to shake. It was something else; something that had been following him for decades.

The room around him was quiet, but the quiet felt wrong, like the world was holding its breath. The wallpaper was yellowing, the floorboards groaning with time, and the musty scent of old wood and dust clung to the air. He lived alone now, save for the occasional visits from his children and grandchildren. But the visits had become infrequent since the drownings began.

The first had been his eldest son, Benjamin, sixty years of age. He had been fishing, a hobby he’d enjoyed all his life. His body was found floating in the river, his face frozen in shock, though he’d been a strong swimmer.

Then came his thirty-six-year-old grandson, Levi, pulled lifeless from the pool behind his suburban home, where his daughter-in-law had only turned away for a moment. Then Sarah, his ten-year-old great-granddaughter, found face down in a shallow pond, despite being too old to wander off carelessly. The drownings were becoming a plague. The deaths were all labeled as tragic accidents, nothing more. But Harrison knew the truth. Each drowning was no accident.

No one believed him, of course. His children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren had stopped visiting, keeping their distance since the deaths began. They called him crazy, whispered behind his back, blamed him; and somewhere deep down, instinctively, they blamed *her*: Evelyn.

He was haunted.

It had begun with her. Evelyn.

He had loved her once, in the early days of their marriage, when her laughter lit up a room and her eyes sparkled with life. She had been so beautiful once, a striking figure in her white lace dress on their wedding day. They were young then, full of hope. But that was before the darkness crept in, before the days of frayed tempers and silent dinners, before the darkness consumed her. Before she wrapped herself in madness and drowned their three children in the lake behind their home.

She had worn her wedding gown that day; a ghostly white dress she once cherished; and led their children into the water, one by one, until the stillness of death settled over the lake. He had found her sitting on the shore, soaked to the bone, staring out at the water as if it had swallowed her whole too. He had burned that dress, torched it until it was nothing but ash, hoping to banish the horror it represented. But no fire could undo what had been done.

She was convicted, of course. Sent away to rot in a cell where she died a few years later, but her death hadn’t been the end. Not for him. He remembered the day she died; not from illness, not from age, but by her own hand. She had drowned herself in her prison cell, using the toilet to end her life. It was grotesque, macabre; she had twisted the white sheets from her bed around herself like some twisted goddess of death, sinking her face into the water until there was no breath left in her. They had found her like that, wrapped in those white linens like a bride of the grave.

The house; the house where it happened; was sold. Harrison couldn’t bear to stay, and so he left. He eventually remarried a woman named Margaret, rebuilt his life, had more children, and tried to move past the tragedy. But Evelyn never truly left him. The haunting began not long after he remarried and moved into a new home with his second wife. No matter how much Harrison tried to forget the horror that had stained his past, Evelyn wouldn’t let him.

He started seeing her in flashes. At first, just glimpses; a figure in white standing in the distance, her face obscured by the shadows. But the closer she came, the more he recognized her; the sharpness of her features, the hollow look in her bloated eyes. She never spoke, never screamed. She didn’t need to. She wore the white sheets every time she appeared to him, her arms wide and beckoning, her hair soaking wet and dripping, her eyes bulging with decay and bloat.

Harrison pressed his trembling fingers against his temple, trying to banish the memories, but they were relentless. She had died, but she hadn’t gone. She haunted him, followed him from one home to the next, always watching, always waiting. And now, she was taking his family.

His thoughts turned to Margaret, who had always believed him. When no one else would listen, when even his own family had called him mad, Margaret stood by him. She had believed him when he told her that Evelyn was still with him, that her ghost followed him from one home to the next. That she wasn’t done.

But Margaret was gone now, too; not dead, not yet, but trapped in a coma from the brain cancer that had stolen her away bit by bit. She had been unresponsive for months, lying in a hospital bed, suspended between life and death, unreachable. Harrison visited her every day. Every single day, without fail. He would sit by her bedside, hold her hand, and talk to her, even if she couldn’t answer. She had always been the only one who believed him.

But now, sitting alone in the darkening room, the feeling of dread gnawed at him. The woman in white had returned with a vengeance, and this time she wasn’t content to haunt only him. She was claiming his family; one by one.

A creak on the stairs pulled him from his thoughts. Harrison froze, the air thick with an unnatural chill. He could feel it; her presence. She was near. His breath caught in his throat as he turned his head slowly, heart pounding against his brittle ribs.

There, at the top of the stairs, she stood, in those waterlogged sheets, her wet hair hanging in limp strands around her pale face, her eyes bulging but fixed on him.

“You thought you could burn it,” she whispered to him, speaking for the first time since her hauntings began. Her voice was a rasp that sent chills down his spine.

He knew she was talking about her wedding gown. The one she had worn when she led their children into the lake all those years ago. She had drowned them one by one, still wearing the gown she had worn on their happiest day, as if trying to sanctify the horror she committed. After the funerals, Harrison had burned the gown in a desperate attempt to rid himself of the nightmare. But no fire could erase what she had done.

“I burned it,” Harrison whispered back, his voice trembling. “I burned it all.”

“But you can’t burn me,” she said, stepping closer, her bare feet leaving wet imprints on the floor as she approached him. “I’m still here, Harrison. I’ll always be here.”

The temperature in the room plummeted, and Harrison felt as though the very walls were closing in. He squeezed his eyes shut, trying to block her out, but it was no use. She had been haunting him for years, and he was powerless to stop her.

“I told you,” he rasped, barely able to find his voice. “I told them… about you. About what you’ve done. But no one believes me. They think I’m crazy.”

Evelyn smiled; a horrible, knowing smile that chilled him to the core. “They always did,” she whispered. “And why wouldn’t they? After all, you remarried, had more children, built a new life. But it doesn’t matter. You’ll lose them all. Just like you lost me.”

He wanted to scream, to tell her to leave him alone, to beg her for mercy. But the words caught in his throat. He could barely breathe.

“Margaret believed me,” he finally managed, his voice hoarse. “She… she knew you were real.”

Evelyn’s smile twisted into something darker, more menacing. “Poor Margaret. She’s all but gone, isn’t she? Trapped in her little world, unable to move, to speak. It’s only a matter of time before she joins the others.”

Harrison’s heart clenched at the thought. Margaret’s children; his children; were all that remained. But for how long? The drownings had already claimed Benjamin, Levi, and Sarah. How many more? How long before Evelyn took them all?

The room fell silent again, save for the faint ticking of the clock on the wall. Evelyn’s presence lingered, cold and suffocating, but she said nothing more. She didn’t need to. She was gone.

Harrison knew what was coming.

Within twenty minutes, in the distance, he could hear the faint wail of sirens, growing louder by the second. His breath caught in his throat as he closed his eyes, already knowing what the news would bring.

Another one.

Another life stolen. Another drowning.

And Evelyn wouldn’t stop; not until she had taken everything from him.

He slumped back in his chair, the weight of despair heavier than ever. He would visit Margaret tomorrow, just as he always did. He would hold her hand and tell her about Evelyn, about the sirens, about how no one believed him anymore.

But she couldn’t answer. And soon, there would be no one left to believe him at all.
